name: Neck training for voice

lead: Some people in looksmaxxing communities train the neck hoping for a thicker-looking neck and a deeper voice. The neck-size payoff is the part most people can see.

Proponents reason that thicker neck muscles change how the neck and larynx work and so lower the voice. No published studies test the voice claim, and standard sources attribute pitch mainly to vocal fold size and laryngeal growth.

paras: People add neck exercises to a regular strength routine and track neck size over months. It is usually combined with general lifting.
No specific risks were documented for the voice claim. Heavy neck exercise carries general injury risks.

web.title: Physical and Visual Characteristics of the Neck Predicting Gender Perception (PMC)

angle.text: The aim is a thicker neck and, per forum claims, a deeper voice as neck muscles grow and change how the larynx sits and works. No published studies test the voice part.

lead: Neck training for voice is the practice, discussed in looksmaxxing communities, of strengthening and thickening the neck muscles in the belief that a bigger, more muscular neck gives a deeper, more resonant voice. Those who try it add neck-strengthening exercises to their training in the hope of a lower-sounding voice, alongside the visual payoff of a thicker neck.

Researchers describe voice pitch as mainly determined by vocal fold length and thickness, which grow under testosterone during puberty along with the larynx and the resonating spaces of the throat, nose and sinuses.[1] A small 2019 study of 15 men and 15 women found that neck girth was the physical measure most associated with pitch and with how masculine a neck and voice were perceived to be, an observational correlation.[2]
No published study was found testing whether training the neck muscles changes voice pitch.
infobox: Thicker neck muscles deepen the voice

paras: Researchers describe voice pitch as mainly determined by vocal fold length and thickness, which grow under testosterone during puberty, along with enlargement of the larynx and the resonating spaces of the face and throat.[1] Wikipedia describes the male voice as reaching adult pitch two to three years after puberty begins and stabilising around ages 21 to 25.[1]

A 2019 study in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery Global Open examined physical and visual characteristics of the neck and how they predicted perceived gender. In 30 speakers, men's neck girth was about 17 to 18 percent larger than women's, girth was the only physical measure that consistently differed between sexes, and it correlated strongly with fundamental frequency (pitch). The authors conclude that voice masculinity relates to a larger neck in girth and width rather than length.[2] The study is small and correlational; it compares men with women and does not test training.
No studies found on neck training and voice. The only related work cited here is the observational neck-girth study, which compares men with women.[2]
